doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Is L.A. studio work craft or soul?
summary: Rowe quotes a colleague that L.A. is craft not soul; Findley says it depends on approach and being versatile.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I have to tell you that you know you made me think, I’ll tell our viewers that we had a 2:00 my time appointment for the Zoom and you dinged me at ten of. And I got this flash of Joe Wilder. You know Joe?

Well he just said this thing, he was so meticulous and such a pro and he talked about how it’s better to be an hour early than a minute late and the whole thing. And anyway that was just an aside. But thanks for the memory, ‘cause I got to know Joe pretty well. I had something I wanted to share with you. I’ve been fortunate to have sessions with a lot of your colleagues. And we were talking, I had a question for one of them who in your phrase will remain anonymous. But I asked him if the L.A. scene, after you’ve done it for a bunch of years ever got tedious or a chore. And he said, “This isn’t playing. It’s craft. L.A. is an incredible place for craft. You really learn to play your instrument well and in tune, to show up on time, the disciplines of the craft are there but your soul, your spirit you know, is not usually nurtured.

Well you know I don’t know if I agree with that. It is a craft, that it is absolutely. But it’s how you take it I think, and how you approach that. You know I’ve come in from one session to another like a minute before and I’ve flown in, get my horn out of the case, sit © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

down and do it and do my job. I think maybe that’s what this person was explaining was doing your job. Yeah you have to do your job and you have to be prepared for it. But you never know what you’re going to get. So being versatile is the answer to that. You have to be versatile. Like I mentioned earlier about Italian vibrato and mariachi vibrato. A Dixieland solo. Bebop, hard bop solo. They’re all different. But you have to be able to do all that because you never know what you’re going to get. But like I said earlier as well is that you know there are players that play notes. That’s — okay that’s what you do you know. And you could be a good section player there. But being a nice person as well in the section, they’re the ones that really need to be nice to be able to be in that section. They could play the part, fine, but I mean there are many, many people that could do that. But as an artist, as a soloist, that’s another thing altogether.
